newsitem.title: ITALY: Pope may be on Islamic extremist hit-list-ANSA.
newsitem.headline: Pope may be on Islamic extremist hit-list-ANSA.

text.p: Italy has put its security forces on alert after an intelligence report that Islamic extremists could be preparing to attack targets including Pope John Paul, the Italian news agency ANSA said on Thursday.
The agency said without quoting sources that the alert was issued at a summit of police and intelligence chiefs at the Interior Ministry on Wednesday night.

The Pope, whose visit last weekend to the Bosnian capital Sarajevo was preceded by the discovery of land mines planted along the route of his motorcade, and international airports in Italy were among potential targets, the agency said.

It said the report sounding the alarm had been drawn up by the Italian military intelligence agency SISMI and referred to the crisis in Europe's relations with Iran as the possible spark for attacks by Islamic militants.
The Interior Ministry declined to comment.
"Vigilance in the face of all possible terrorist threats is permanent and systematic," the ministry said in a statement.
Citing the need for "maximum reserve" it said "indiscretions and alarmism can only harm the cause of public security".
The Vatican initially also declined comment but its Secretary of State, Cardinal Angelo Sodano, later told Italian television that the Pope was not "particularly alarmed".
"These (news) reports have also reached us but the attitude of me and my colleagues and above all of the Holy Father is as it always was," Sodano said.
"We all trust in the Italian authorities...and we all pray for the Holy Father that Divine Providence will protect and safeguard him as it has throughout all these years," he said.
The Pope, 76, was almost killed in 1981 in an attack in St Peter's Square by Turkish gunman Mehmet Ali Agca, who is now serving a life sentence in an Italian jail.

The Roman Catholic leader continued with his Sarajevo visit despite the discovery of the 23 land mines, planted under a road bridge into Sarajevo from the airport. The mines, attached to a detonator, were defused a few hours before he arrived.

All European Union countries except Greece recalled their ambassadors from Iran last week for consultations after a German court found that the Iranian leadership had ordered the 1992 killing of four Kurdish opposition activists in Berlin.
The verdict prompted an official protest from Iran and unleashed a wave of demonstrations in Tehran where thousands of people took to the streets.
